title: Engineering Thermodynamics
description: Systems and properties, steam tables and quality, ideal gases, boundary work, the first law for closed systems and flow devices, second law and Carnot limits, entropy and isentropic efficiency, exergy, Otto, Diesel, Brayton, Rankine and refrigeration cycles, moist air and combustion basics.

cards.title: What type of thermodynamic system allows neither mass nor energy to cross its boundary?
cards.body:
An isolated system.

**Closed system** (control mass): energy can cross as heat or work, but mass cannot, e.g., gas in a piston–cylinder.

**Open system** (control volume): both mass and energy cross, e.g., turbines, nozzles, pumps.

Tip: a rigid, perfectly insulated sealed tank is isolated; the whole universe is the ultimate isolated system.
cards.searchQuery: isolated system definition closed open thermodynamics

cards.title: Are heat and work state (point) functions or path functions, and what does that mean?
cards.body:
Path functions.

Heat and work are **path functions**: their amounts depend on the process path, not just the end states. Properties ($P$, $T$, $v$, $u$, $h$, $s$) are **state functions**.

For a cycle, $\oint dU = 0$, while the net work generally isn't zero.

Key idea: write $\delta Q$ and $\delta W$ (inexact differentials) and $Q_{12}$ or $W_{12}$.
Watch out: never write $\Delta Q$ or $\Delta W$; only properties have a $\Delta$.
cards.searchQuery: heat and work path functions vs state functions properties

cards.title: A closed system receives $50\,\mathrm{kJ}$ of heat and does $20\,\mathrm{kJ}$ of work on its surroundings. What is $\Delta U$, in kJ? (No KE or PE change.)
cards.body:
$\Delta U = +30\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

Sign convention used (Çengel): $Q - W = \Delta U + \Delta\mathrm{KE} + \Delta\mathrm{PE}$, with $Q$ = **net heat transfer TO the system** and $W$ = net work **done BY the system**: $50 - 20 = 30\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

Many chemistry texts write $\Delta U = Q + W$ with $W$ done ON the system: same physics, opposite sign on $W$.

Tip: label each sign (heat in is +, work out is +) before substituting numbers.
cards.searchQuery: first law closed system delta U heat work sign convention

cards.title: What is the quality $x$ of a saturated liquid–vapor mixture, and how do you find it from the specific volume $v$?
cards.body:
$x = m_{\text{vapor}}/m_{\text{total}}$ ($0$ = saturated liquid, $1$ = saturated vapor); it's defined only under the **vapor dome**.

$v = v_f + x\,v_{fg}$, so $x = \dfrac{v - v_f}{v_g - v_f}$. Same pattern for $u$, $h$ and $s$.

Example: water at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$: $v_f = 0.001043$ and $v_g = 1.6720\,\mathrm{m^3/kg}$, so $v = 0.5\,\mathrm{m^3/kg}$ gives $x \approx 0.30$.
cards.searchQuery: quality of saturated liquid vapor mixture steam tables

cards.title: For an ideal gas, what does $c_p - c_v$ equal?
cards.body:
$c_p - c_v = R$, the **specific gas constant** ($R = R_u/M$, with $R_u = 8.314\,\mathrm{kJ/(kmol\cdot K)}$).

Air: $R = 0.287$, $c_p \approx 1.005$ and $c_v \approx 0.718\,\mathrm{kJ/(kg\cdot K)}$ at room temperature, so $k = c_p/c_v \approx 1.4$.

Ideal-gas $u$ and $h$ depend on $T$ only: $\Delta u = c_v\,\Delta T$ and $\Delta h = c_p\,\Delta T$ for ANY process (constant specific heats), not just constant-volume or constant-pressure ones.

Key idea: $c_p > c_v$ for any gas, and the gap equals $R$ for an ideal gas.
cards.searchQuery: ideal gas cp minus cv equals R

cards.title: Boundary work done by an ideal gas expanding isothermally in a closed system from $V_1$ to $V_2$?
cards.body:
$W_b = mRT\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} = P_1V_1\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} = mRT\ln\dfrac{P_1}{P_2}$.

It's $\int P\,dV$ with $P = mRT/V$. In general $W_b$ is the **area under the process curve** on a $P$–$V$ diagram (constant $P$: $W_b = P(V_2 - V_1)$; $1\,\mathrm{kPa\cdot m^3} = 1\,\mathrm{kJ}$).

Isothermal ideal gas: $\Delta U = 0$, so $Q = W_b$.

Watch out: use absolute $T$ in $mRT$, and $V_2/V_1$ (or $P_1/P_2$) inside the log, never a difference.
cards.searchQuery: isothermal ideal gas boundary work mRT ln V2/V1

cards.title: Why do control-volume (open-system) energy balances use enthalpy $h$ instead of internal energy $u$?
cards.body:
Because $h = u + Pv$ includes the **flow work**.

$Pv$ is the energy needed to push each kilogram of fluid across the boundary. So each unit mass of flowing fluid carries energy $h + \dfrac{V^2}{2} + gz$.

Example: for an ideal gas, $\Delta h = c_p\,\Delta T$.
Tip: for a closed system at constant pressure with only boundary work, $Q = \Delta H$.
cards.searchQuery: enthalpy flow work open system control volume h = u + Pv

cards.title: Air enters an adiabatic nozzle at negligible velocity, and its enthalpy drops by $20\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$. What is the exit velocity, in m/s?
cards.body:
$V_2 = 200\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

**Steady flow**, no work or heat, $\Delta\mathrm{PE} \approx 0$: $\dfrac{V_2^2}{2} = h_1 - h_2 = 20\,\mathrm{kJ/kg} = 20{,}000\,\mathrm{m^2/s^2}$, so $V_2 = \sqrt{40{,}000} = 200\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Watch out: forgetting $1\,\mathrm{kJ/kg} = 1000\,\mathrm{m^2/s^2}$ gives $\sqrt{40} \approx 6.3\,\mathrm{m/s}$. A diffuser does the reverse: it slows the flow and raises $h$ and $P$.
cards.searchQuery: adiabatic nozzle exit velocity from enthalpy drop

cards.title: Across an adiabatic throttling valve (no work, negligible KE and PE change), which property stays constant?
cards.body:
**Enthalpy**: $h_1 = h_2$ (isenthalpic).

For an ideal gas $h = h(T)$, so $T$ stays constant too. A real fluid such as a refrigerant drops sharply in pressure and temperature, partly flashing to vapor: that's the **expansion valve** in a refrigerator.

Entropy increases: throttling is highly irreversible.

Tip: on a $P$–$h$ or $T$–$s$ chart, a throttling process is a vertical line on $P$–$h$ (constant $h$).

cards.title: State the Kelvin–Planck and the Clausius statements of the second law.
cards.body:
Kelvin–Planck: no cyclic device can produce net work while exchanging heat with a single reservoir.

**Kelvin–Planck:** no heat engine can have $\eta_{\text{th}} = 100\%$.

**Clausius:** no cyclic device can have, as its sole effect, heat transfer from a colder body to a hotter one, so a refrigerator needs a work input.

Key idea: the two statements are equivalent; violating one violates the other.
cards.searchQuery: Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements of the second law

cards.title: Maximum possible thermal efficiency of a heat engine operating between reservoirs at $527\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $27\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, in percent?
cards.body:
$62.5\%$.

$\eta_{\text{Carnot}} = 1 - \dfrac{T_L}{T_H}$ with **ABSOLUTE temperatures**: $1 - \dfrac{300\,\mathrm{K}}{800\,\mathrm{K}} = 0.625$.

Watch out: plugging in Celsius gives $1 - 27/527 \approx 95\%$. Every real (irreversible) engine between the same two reservoirs does worse.
cards.searchQuery: Carnot efficiency 1 - TL/TH absolute temperature

cards.title: A refrigeration cycle has $\mathrm{COP_R} = 3$. What is its COP when the same cycle (same $Q_L$, $Q_H$, $W$) is used as a heat pump?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{COP_{HP}} = 4$.

$\mathrm{COP_R} = Q_L/W_{\text{in}}$ and $\mathrm{COP_{HP}} = Q_H/W_{\text{in}} = (Q_L + W_{\text{in}})/W_{\text{in}} = \mathrm{COP_R} + 1$.

COPs above 1 are normal; **COP isn't an efficiency**. Reversible (Carnot) limits, with absolute temperatures: $\mathrm{COP_{R,rev}} = \dfrac{T_L}{T_H - T_L}$ and $\mathrm{COP_{HP,rev}} = \dfrac{T_H}{T_H - T_L}$.

Tip: $\mathrm{COP_{HP}} = \mathrm{COP_R} + 1$ holds for the same cycle operated either way.
cards.searchQuery: heat pump COP equals refrigerator COP plus 1

cards.title: An analysis of a proposed process gives entropy generation $S_{\text{gen}} < 0$. What can you conclude?
cards.body:
The process is **impossible**: it violates the second law.

$S_{\text{gen}} > 0$: **irreversible** (every real process); $S_{\text{gen}} = 0$: reversible (an idealization); $S_{\text{gen}} < 0$: impossible.

Watch out: a system's own entropy CAN decrease when heat leaves it. Only $S_{\text{gen}}$, equivalently $\Delta S$ of an isolated system, can never be negative.
cards.searchQuery: entropy generation negative impossible second law

cards.title: For an ideal gas with constant specific heats undergoing an isentropic process, what combination of $P$ and $V$ stays constant?
cards.body:
$PV^k$ (equivalently $Pv^k$), with $k = c_p/c_v \approx 1.4$ for air.

Also $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \left(\dfrac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{(k-1)/k} = \left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right)^{k-1}$.

A **reversible adiabatic** process is isentropic.

Watch out: $PV = \text{constant}$ is the isothermal ideal-gas process, not the isentropic one.
cards.searchQuery: isentropic ideal gas PV^k constant

cards.title: Cold-air-standard Otto cycle: thermal efficiency in terms of compression ratio $r$ and specific heat ratio $k$?
cards.body:
$\eta_{\text{Otto}} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{r^{k-1}}$.

$r = V_{\text{max}}/V_{\text{min}}$.

Efficiency rises with $r$, but real spark-ignition engines can't raise $r$ much because of **engine knock** (autoignition of the fuel–air mixture).

Example: $r = 8$, $k = 1.4$ gives $1 - 8^{-0.4} \approx 0.565$ ($56.5\%$).
cards.searchQuery: Otto cycle thermal efficiency compression ratio

cards.title: List the four components of the ideal Rankine cycle in flow order, with the ideal process in each.
cards.body:
Pump, boiler, turbine, condenser.

1. Pump: isentropic compression of liquid
2. Boiler: constant-pressure heat addition
3. Turbine: isentropic expansion
4. Condenser: constant-pressure heat rejection

$\eta_{\text{th}} = \dfrac{w_{\text{net}}}{q_{\text{in}}} = 1 - \dfrac{q_{\text{out}}}{q_{\text{in}}}$.

Why: the liquid's specific volume is small, so pump work $w_{\text{pump}} \approx v(P_2 - P_1)$ is tiny next to turbine work.
cards.searchQuery: ideal Rankine cycle four components processes pump boiler turbine condenser

cards.title: Is specific volume $v$ an intensive or an extensive property?
cards.body:
**Intensive**: it doesn't depend on the size of the system.

Volume $V$, mass $m$ and total energy $E$ are **extensive**; dividing an extensive property by mass gives an intensive specific property: $v = V/m$, $u = U/m$, $h = H/m$.

Quick test: split the system in half. Properties that halve are extensive; those that stay the same ($T$, $P$, $\rho$, $v$) are intensive.

Mnemonic: extensive properties **extend** with size; intensive ones stay **intense** (the same) everywhere.
cards.searchQuery: intensive vs extensive properties specific volume

cards.title: State postulate: how many independent intensive properties fix the state of a simple compressible system?
cards.body:
Two.

**Any two independent intensive properties** (e.g., $T$ and $v$, or $P$ and $h$) fix all the others.

Watch out: inside the vapor dome, $T$ and $P$ are NOT independent ($T = T_{\text{sat}}$ at the given $P$), so they can't fix the state of a saturated mixture; you also need $x$, $v$, $h$ or similar.
cards.searchQuery: state postulate independent intensive properties simple compressible

cards.title: What does the zeroth law of thermodynamics state?
cards.body:
Two bodies in thermal equilibrium with a third are in thermal equilibrium with each other.

It's the basis of **temperature measurement**: the thermometer is the third body, and bodies in thermal equilibrium have the same temperature.

Key idea: the zeroth law is what makes "temperature" a well-defined property.
cards.searchQuery: zeroth law of thermodynamics thermal equilibrium temperature

cards.title: Convert $32\,^\circ\mathrm{F}$ to the Rankine scale. Give the number in R, to two decimal places.
cards.body:
$491.67\,\mathrm{R}$.

$T\,[\mathrm{R}] = T\,[{}^\circ\mathrm{F}] + 459.67$, just as $T\,[\mathrm{K}] = T\,[{}^\circ\mathrm{C}] + 273.15$. Rankine is the **absolute scale** in English units: $T\,[\mathrm{R}] = 1.8\,T\,[\mathrm{K}]$.

For temperature differences, $1\,\mathrm{K}$ equals $1\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $1\,\mathrm{R}$ equals $1\,^\circ\mathrm{F}$, so $\Delta T\,[\mathrm{R}] = 1.8\,\Delta T\,[\mathrm{K}]$.

Tip: for $T\,[\mathrm{K}]$ use $273.15$; for $T\,[\mathrm{R}]$ use $459.67$.
cards.searchQuery: convert Fahrenheit to Rankine absolute temperature

cards.title: A tire gauge reads $200\,\mathrm{kPa}$ where $P_{\text{atm}} = 100\,\mathrm{kPa}$. What pressure, in kPa, goes into the ideal-gas law?
cards.body:
$300\,\mathrm{kPa}$ (absolute).

$P_{\text{abs}} = P_{\text{gage}} + P_{\text{atm}} = 200 + 100 = 300\,\mathrm{kPa}$. The ideal-gas law and the property tables always use **absolute pressure** and absolute temperature (K or R).

Watch out: plugging in the gauge reading understates the mass of air in the tire by a third.
cards.searchQuery: gauge pressure to absolute pressure ideal gas law

cards.title: Can the temperature of a closed system change during an adiabatic process?
cards.body:
Yes. **Adiabatic means** $Q = 0$, not $\Delta T = 0$.

Work can still change the internal energy: compressing a gas adiabatically raises its temperature ($\Delta U = -W_b > 0$), and an adiabatic expansion cools it.

Watch out: don't confuse adiabatic ($Q = 0$) with isothermal ($T$ constant).
cards.searchQuery: adiabatic process temperature change compression heating

cards.title: No compressed-liquid table? Approximate a compressed liquid's $v$, $u$ and $h$ with saturated-liquid values at the same pressure, or at the same temperature?
cards.body:
At the **same temperature**: $v \approx v_{f@T}$, $u \approx u_{f@T}$, $h \approx h_{f@T}$.

Liquid properties depend much more on temperature than on pressure. A better estimate for enthalpy adds a pressure correction: $h \approx h_{f@T} + v_{f@T}\,(P - P_{\text{sat}@T})$.

Watch out: taking $h_f$ at the given pressure can be badly off.
cards.searchQuery: compressed liquid approximation saturated liquid same temperature

cards.title: Water is at $200\,\mathrm{kPa}$ and $150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$; $T_{\text{sat}}$ at $200\,\mathrm{kPa}$ is $120.21\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. What phase is it in?
cards.body:
Superheated vapor, because $T > T_{\text{sat}@P}$.

At a given $P$: $T < T_{\text{sat}}$ means **compressed (subcooled) liquid**; $T > T_{\text{sat}}$ means **superheated vapor**; $T = T_{\text{sat}}$ means a saturated state, which needs a second property such as $x$ or $v$.

Equivalently, at a given $T$: $P > P_{\text{sat}}$ means compressed liquid.

Tip: look up $T_{\text{sat}}$ at the given pressure first, then compare.
cards.searchQuery: determine phase from pressure and temperature steam superheated

cards.title: What is the critical temperature of water, in °C, to the nearest degree?
cards.body:
$374\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($373.95\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$); the critical pressure is $22.06\,\mathrm{MPa}$.

At the **critical point** $v_f = v_g$ and $h_{fg} = 0$. Above it there's no distinct boiling: the liquid turns into vapor gradually, without a two-phase region.

Supercritical steam power plants run their boilers above $22.06\,\mathrm{MPa}$.

Key idea: above $T_{\text{cr}}$ no pressure can liquefy the vapor.
cards.searchQuery: critical point of water temperature pressure

cards.title: At what temperature, in °C, can ice, liquid water and water vapor coexist in equilibrium?
cards.body:
$0.01\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (the **triple point**), at a pressure of $0.6117\,\mathrm{kPa}$.

Below the triple-point pressure, liquid can't exist: ice sublimates directly to vapor, which is how freeze-drying works.

The triple point is a single point on a $P$–$T$ diagram but a line on $P$–$v$ and $T$–$v$ diagrams.

Key idea: the triple point of water ($273.16\,\mathrm{K}$) was historically used to define the kelvin.
cards.searchQuery: triple point of water temperature pressure

cards.title: What does $h_{fg}$ in the steam tables represent, and what happens to it as the saturation pressure rises?
cards.body:
The enthalpy of vaporization (latent heat), $h_{fg} = h_g - h_f$.

It's the energy needed to vaporize a unit mass of saturated liquid at constant $T$ and $P$. It **decreases** as saturation pressure rises and reaches zero at the critical point.

Example: $h_{fg} = 2256.4\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$ for water at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
cards.searchQuery: enthalpy of vaporization hfg latent heat steam tables

cards.title: Water at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ has quality $x = 0.5$. With $h_f = 419.17$ and $h_{fg} = 2256.4\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$, what is $h$, in kJ/kg to the nearest whole number?
cards.body:
$h \approx 1547\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$.

$h = h_f + x\,h_{fg} = 419.17 + 0.5(2256.4) = 1547.4\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$.

Watch out: $h = x\,h_g$ **ignores the liquid's enthalpy**. Use $h_f + x\,h_{fg}$, or equivalently $(1 - x)h_f + x\,h_g$.
cards.searchQuery: enthalpy of saturated mixture h = hf + x hfg

cards.title: A steam table lists $h = 3051.6\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$ at $300\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $3158.2$ at $350\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (same $P$). Interpolate $h$ at $320\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, in kJ/kg to one decimal.
cards.body:
$h \approx 3094.2\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$.

**Linear interpolation**: $h = h_1 + \dfrac{T - T_1}{T_2 - T_1}(h_2 - h_1) = 3051.6 + \dfrac{20}{50}(106.6) = 3051.6 + 42.64$.

Sanity check: $320\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is $40\%$ of the way from 300 to 350, so $h$ must be $40\%$ of the way from 3051.6 to 3158.2.

Tip: interpolate between the two rows that bracket your value; never extrapolate far outside the table.
cards.searchQuery: linear interpolation steam tables enthalpy

cards.title: Compressibility factor $Z = \dfrac{Pv}{RT}$: near what state does a real gas deviate most from ideal-gas behavior ($Z = 1$)?
cards.body:
Near the critical point (and generally close to the saturated-vapor line).

By the principle of corresponding states, $Z$ is about the same function of reduced pressure $P_R = P/P_{\text{cr}}$ and reduced temperature $T_R = T/T_{\text{cr}}$ for all gases: the **generalized compressibility chart**.

The ideal-gas model works well when $P_R \ll 1$ at any temperature, or when $T_R > 2$ unless $P_R \gg 1$.

Key idea: $Z = 1$ means ideal-gas behavior; $Z < 1$ means attractive forces dominate.
cards.searchQuery: compressibility factor Z real gas deviation critical point

cards.title: Using $R = 0.287\,\mathrm{kJ/(kg\cdot K)}$, what is the density of air at $100\,\mathrm{kPa}$ and $300\,\mathrm{K}$, in $\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ to two decimals?
cards.body:
$\rho \approx 1.16\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.

$\rho = \dfrac{P}{RT} = \dfrac{100}{(0.287)(300)} = 1.161\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$. The units work because $1\,\mathrm{**kPa**} = 1\,\mathrm{kJ/m^3}$.

Watch out: $P$ in kPa with $R$ in $\mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)}$ gives an answer $1000$ times too small.
cards.searchQuery: density of air ideal gas law P/RT

cards.title: With $R_u = 8.314\,\mathrm{kJ/(kmol\cdot K)}$, what is the gas constant of helium ($M = 4.003\,\mathrm{kg/kmol}$), in $\mathrm{kJ/(kg\cdot K)}$ to three decimals?
cards.body:
$R \approx 2.077\,\mathrm{kJ/(kg\cdot K)}$.

$R = R_u/M = 8.314/4.003 = 2.0769$. Each gas has its own $R$, while $R_u$ is the same for all gases.

**Light gases** have large $R$: helium's is about 7 times that of air ($0.287$).

Watch out: $R_u = 8.314\,\mathrm{kJ/(kmol\cdot K)}$ is universal; $R$ in $Pv = RT$ is the one for your gas.
cards.searchQuery: specific gas constant helium R = Ru/M

cards.title: What is the specific heat ratio $k = c_p/c_v$ of a monatomic ideal gas such as helium or argon?
cards.body:
$k = 5/3 \approx 1.667$.

A **monatomic** gas stores energy only as translational kinetic energy: $\bar{c}_v = \tfrac{3}{2}R_u$ and $\bar{c}_p = \tfrac{5}{2}R_u$ on a molar basis, independent of temperature.

Diatomic gases such as air near room temperature: $\bar{c}_v \approx \tfrac{5}{2}R_u$, so $k \approx 1.4$.

Key idea: more molecular degrees of freedom means a smaller $k$ (monatomic $5/3$, diatomic $7/5$).
cards.searchQuery: specific heat ratio monatomic ideal gas 5/3

cards.title: Why is $c_p$ larger than $c_v$ for a gas?
cards.body:
At constant pressure the gas expands as it's heated, so part of the heat input leaves as **boundary work** instead of raising $u$.

At constant volume there's no boundary work, so all the heat raises the internal energy. For an ideal gas the difference is exactly $c_p - c_v = R$.

For nearly incompressible liquids and solids, $c_p \approx c_v = c$.

Key idea: constant-pressure heating must supply both the internal-energy rise and the expansion work.
cards.searchQuery: why cp greater than cv constant pressure heating

cards.title: A gas in a piston–cylinder device expands at a constant $200\,\mathrm{kPa}$ from $0.1$ to $0.4\,\mathrm{m^3}$. Boundary work done by the gas, in kJ?
cards.body:
$W_b = 60\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

$W_b = P(V_2 - V_1) = (200\,\mathrm{kPa})(0.3\,\mathrm{m^3}) = 60\,\mathrm{kPa\cdot m^3} = 60\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

It's **positive** because the gas does work on the surroundings as it expands. On a $P$–$V$ diagram it's the rectangle under the horizontal process line.

Tip: $1\,\mathrm{kPa\cdot m^3} = 1\,\mathrm{kJ}$, so no unit conversion is needed with kPa and $\mathrm{m^3}$.
cards.searchQuery: constant pressure boundary work P delta V kJ

cards.title: Boundary work for a polytropic process $PV^n = C$ with $n \ne 1$, from state 1 to state 2?
cards.body:
$W_b = \dfrac{P_2V_2 - P_1V_1}{1 - n}$, which for an ideal gas equals $\dfrac{mR(T_2 - T_1)}{1 - n}$.

It comes from $\int P\,dV$ with $P = CV^{-n}$. The case $n = 1$ needs the **log form**, $W_b = P_1V_1\ln(V_2/V_1)$.

Sign check: an expansion ($V_2 > V_1$) gives $W_b > 0$ for any $n$.

Watch out: this formula divides by $1 - n$, so it fails at $n = 1$; use the logarithmic form there.
cards.searchQuery: polytropic process boundary work formula

cards.title: In the polytropic relation $Pv^n = \text{constant}$, which value of $n$ describes a constant-volume process?
cards.body:
$n \to \infty$.

Take the $n$th root: $P^{1/n}v = \text{constant}$, and as $n \to \infty$ this becomes $v = \text{constant}$.

Other cases: $n = 0$ is constant pressure, $n = 1$ is **isothermal** (ideal gas), and $n = k$ is isentropic (ideal gas with constant specific heats).

Tip: for an ideal gas, think of $n$ as a dial: $0$ (isobaric), $1$ (isothermal), $k$ (isentropic), $\infty$ (isochoric).
cards.searchQuery: polytropic exponent n constant volume constant pressure isothermal

cards.title: An ideal gas is compressed isothermally in a closed system. What is its change in internal energy, $\Delta U$?
cards.body:
$\Delta U = 0$: ideal-gas $u$ **depends only on** $T$.

So the first law gives $Q = W_b$: the work done on the gas leaves as heat ($W_b < 0$ and $Q < 0$).

Watch out: this holds for an ideal gas, not for a phase change at constant $T$ (like boiling water), where $u$ changes a lot.
cards.searchQuery: isothermal compression ideal gas change in internal energy zero

cards.title: $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ of air in a rigid tank is heated from $300$ to $400\,\mathrm{K}$ ($c_v = 0.718\,\mathrm{kJ/(kg\cdot K)}$). How much heat is added, in kJ to one decimal?
cards.body:
$Q = 143.6\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

**Rigid tank**: $W_b = 0$, so $Q = \Delta U = mc_v\,\Delta T = 2(0.718)(100) = 143.6\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

Watch out: using $c_p = 1.005$ gives $201\,\mathrm{kJ}$, which would be right only for a constant-pressure process with only boundary work.
cards.searchQuery: rigid tank heating Q = m cv delta T

cards.title: An ideal gas fills half of an insulated rigid tank and expands freely into the evacuated other half. How does its final temperature compare with its initial one?
cards.body:
It's the same.

$W = 0$ (the gas pushes against nothing, and the tank is rigid) and $Q = 0$ (insulated), so $\Delta U = 0$, and for an ideal gas that means $\Delta T = 0$.

The process is still **irreversible**: the entropy rises by $mR\ln 2$ as the volume doubles.

Watch out: the temperature stays constant only for an ideal gas; a real gas changes temperature slightly.
cards.searchQuery: free expansion ideal gas temperature unchanged

cards.title: A heat engine receives $500\,\mathrm{kJ}$ of heat and rejects $300\,\mathrm{kJ}$ per cycle. What is its thermal efficiency, in percent?
cards.body:
$\eta_{\text{th}} = 40\%$.

Over a cycle $\Delta U = 0$, so $W_{\text{net}} = Q_H - Q_L = 200\,\mathrm{kJ}$ and $\eta_{\text{th}} = \dfrac{W_{\text{net}}}{Q_H} = \dfrac{200}{500} = 0.40$.

Equivalently $\eta_{\text{th}} = 1 - Q_L/Q_H$.

Watch out: dividing by the heat rejected instead of the **heat received**.
cards.searchQuery: heat engine thermal efficiency work over heat input

cards.title: Specific heats are tabulated in $\mathrm{kJ/(kg\cdot K)}$. Can you multiply them by a temperature change measured in °C?
cards.body:
Yes: a change of $1\,\mathrm{K}$ equals a change of $1\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, so $\Delta T$ is the same number on both scales.

What you can't do is use Celsius values where absolute temperature appears on its own: $Pv = RT$, $T_L/T_H$, $\ln(T_2/T_1)$ and $T_0S_{\text{gen}}$ all need **kelvins** (or rankines).

Tip: use whichever scale you like for $\Delta T$, but kelvins whenever $T$ appears in a ratio or logarithm.
cards.searchQuery: temperature difference Celsius Kelvin specific heat units

cards.title: Steam with specific volume $0.5\,\mathrm{m^3/kg}$ flows at $30\,\mathrm{m/s}$ through a pipe of cross-section $0.05\,\mathrm{m^2}$. Mass flow rate, in kg/s?
cards.body:
$\dot{m} = 3\,\mathrm{kg/s}$.

$\dot{m} = \rho VA = \dfrac{VA}{v} = \dfrac{(30)(0.05)}{0.5} = 3\,\mathrm{kg/s}$.

In **steady flow** $\dot{m}$ is the same at every section, but the volume flow rate $\dot{V} = \dot{m}v$ changes wherever $v$ does, e.g., as steam expands through a turbine.

Tip: $\dot{m} = \rho V A = VA/v$; use whichever of $\rho$ or $v$ the table gives.
cards.searchQuery: mass flow rate rho V A specific volume steam

cards.title: Write the steady-flow energy equation for a control volume with one inlet (1) and one outlet (2).
cards.body:
$$\dot{Q} - \dot{W} = \dot{m}\left[h_2 - h_1 + \frac{V_2^2 - V_1^2}{2} + g(z_2 - z_1)\right]$$

$\dot{Q}$ is the heat transfer **in** and $\dot{W}$ is the shaft or electrical power **out**; flow work is already inside $h$.

Per unit mass: $q - w = \Delta h + \Delta\mathrm{ke} + \Delta\mathrm{pe}$.

Watch out: $V^2/2$ comes out in $\mathrm{J/kg}$, while $h$ is usually in $\mathrm{kJ/kg}$.
cards.searchQuery: steady flow energy equation control volume one inlet one outlet

cards.title: Steam flows at $2\,\mathrm{kg/s}$ through an adiabatic turbine, entering with $h = 3200$ and leaving with $h = 2700\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$ (negligible KE, PE). Power output, in kW?
cards.body:
$\dot{W}_{\text{out}} = 1000\,\mathrm{kW}$ ($1\,\mathrm{MW}$).

$\dot{W}_{\text{out}} = \dot{m}(h_1 - h_2) = 2(3200 - 2700) = 1000\,\mathrm{kW}$, since $\mathrm{**kg/s**} \times \mathrm{kJ/kg} = \mathrm{kJ/s} = \mathrm{kW}$.

Any heat loss from the turbine would make the work output smaller than the enthalpy drop.

Tip: $\mathrm{kg/s} \times \mathrm{kJ/kg} = \mathrm{kW}$, so no conversion is needed.
cards.searchQuery: steam turbine power output mass flow enthalpy drop

cards.title: A steam turbine ($\dot{m} = 1\,\mathrm{kg/s}$, $h_1 - h_2 = 600\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$, negligible KE and PE changes) loses $20\,\mathrm{kW}$ of heat. Power output, in kW?
cards.body:
$\dot{W}_{\text{out}} = 580\,\mathrm{kW}$.

**Energy balance**: $\dot{Q} - \dot{W} = \dot{m}(h_2 - h_1)$ with $\dot{Q} = -20\,\mathrm{kW}$ because the heat leaves: $\dot{W} = -20 + 600 = 580\,\mathrm{kW}$.

Watch out: adding the heat loss to the work ($620\,\mathrm{kW}$). Energy lost as heat can't also come out as work.
cards.searchQuery: turbine with heat loss energy balance power output

cards.title: Air ($c_p = 1.005\,\mathrm{kJ/(kg\cdot K)}$) flows at $0.5\,\mathrm{kg/s}$ through an adiabatic compressor and heats from $300$ to $450\,\mathrm{K}$. Power input, in kW to one decimal?
cards.body:
$\dot{W}_{\text{in}} \approx 75.4\,\mathrm{kW}$.

$\dot{W}_{\text{in}} = \dot{m}c_p(T_2 - T_1) = 0.5(1.005)(150) = 75.4\,\mathrm{kW}$, neglecting KE and PE changes.

Use $c_p$, not $c_v$: in a flow device the energy change is an **enthalpy change**, which includes flow work.

Watch out: a real compressor's exit is hotter than the isentropic one, so this $\Delta T$ is what includes the losses.
cards.searchQuery: adiabatic compressor power input air cp delta T

cards.title: Water ($v = 0.001\,\mathrm{m^3/kg}$) is pumped reversibly and adiabatically from $100\,\mathrm{kPa}$ to $5\,\mathrm{MPa}$. Pump work, in kJ/kg?
cards.body:
$w_{\text{pump}} = 4.9\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$.

For an **incompressible liquid**, $w_{\text{rev}} = \int v\,dP = v(P_2 - P_1) = 0.001(5000 - 100) = 4.9\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$, using $\mathrm{m^3/kg} \times \mathrm{kPa} = \mathrm{kJ/kg}$.

Watch out: forgetting to convert MPa to kPa. Compressing vapor over the same range would take far more work, because its $v$ is far larger.
cards.searchQuery: pump work incompressible liquid v delta P

cards.title: Insulated heat exchanger: hot water at $2\,\mathrm{kg/s}$ cools from $80$ to $60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$; cold water at $4\,\mathrm{kg/s}$ enters at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Cold exit temperature, in °C?
cards.body:
$30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

**Heat lost by the hot stream** = heat gained by the cold stream, with the same $c_p$: $2(80 - 60) = 4(T_{\text{out}} - 20)$, so $T_{\text{out}} = 30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

The streams don't mix. For the whole exchanger $\dot{Q} = 0$ and $\dot{W} = 0$, but for each stream alone there is heat transfer.

Tip: this works because both streams are water; with different fluids use $\dot{m}c_p\,\Delta T$ for each.
cards.searchQuery: heat exchanger energy balance outlet temperature

cards.title: In an adiabatic mixing chamber, $1\,\mathrm{kg/s}$ of water at $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ mixes with $3\,\mathrm{kg/s}$ at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Exit temperature, in °C (constant $c_p$)?
cards.body:
$35\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Energy balance: $\sum \dot{m}_{\text{in}}h_{\text{in}} = \dot{m}_{\text{out}}h_{\text{out}}$, so with constant $c_p$ the exit temperature is the **mass-weighted average**: $\dfrac{1(80) + 3(20)}{4} = 35\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Watch out: the plain average, $50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, ignores the flow rates.
cards.searchQuery: adiabatic mixing chamber exit temperature mass weighted

cards.title: An insulated, evacuated rigid tank fills from a supply line carrying air at $300\,\mathrm{K}$. Final air temperature in the tank, in K? ($k = 1.4$, constant specific heats.)
cards.body:
$420\,\mathrm{K}$.

Unsteady energy balance with $Q = W = 0$ and an empty tank at the start: $m_2u_2 = m_2h_{\text{line}}$, so $c_vT_2 = c_pT_{\text{line}}$ and $T_2 = kT_{\text{line}} = 1.4(300) = 420\,\mathrm{K}$.

The air gets hotter because the **flow work** that pushes it into the tank becomes internal energy.

Watch out: the final temperature is higher than the line temperature, even though the tank is insulated.
cards.searchQuery: tank filling unsteady energy balance final temperature kT

cards.title: What is the kinetic energy per unit mass of a stream moving at $45\,\mathrm{m/s}$, in kJ/kg to two decimals?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{ke} \approx 1.01\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$.

$\mathrm{ke} = \dfrac{V^2}{2} = \dfrac{45^2}{2} = 1012.5\,\mathrm{J/kg}$.

That's tiny next to the hundreds of kJ/kg of enthalpy change in turbines and boilers, so $\Delta\mathrm{ke}$ is usually neglected there, but not in **nozzles and diffusers**, whose whole job is to change velocity.

Tip: $V^2/2$ in $\mathrm{m^2/s^2}$ equals $\mathrm{J/kg}$; divide by $1000$ to get $\mathrm{kJ/kg}$.
cards.searchQuery: kinetic energy per unit mass V squared over 2 kJ/kg

cards.title: Take a sealed, insulated room with an electric heater inside as the system. Is the electrical energy entering through the wires heat or work?
cards.body:
Work (electrical work, $W_e = VI\,\Delta t$).

**Heat is energy that crosses a boundary** because of a temperature difference, and the electrical energy doesn't.

If you instead take only the room air as the system, the hot heater coil transfers heat to it.

Key idea: whether energy counts as heat or work depends on where you draw the system boundary.
cards.searchQuery: electrical energy heat or work system boundary

cards.title: A device claims to produce net work in a cycle while exchanging heat with only one reservoir. What kind of perpetual-motion machine is it?
cards.body:
A **perpetual-motion machine of the second kind** (PMM2): it violates the Kelvin–Planck statement of the second law.

A perpetual-motion machine of the first kind creates energy, violating the first law.

Every real heat engine must reject some heat to a lower-temperature sink.

Key idea: PMM2 satisfies the first law but violates the second; PMM1 violates the first.
cards.searchQuery: perpetual motion machine second kind Kelvin-Planck

cards.title: Name common sources of irreversibility that make real processes fall short of reversible ones.
cards.body:
Friction, heat transfer across a finite temperature difference, free expansion, mixing, resistance heating, inelastic deformation and chemical reactions.

Each one generates entropy ($S_{\text{gen}} > 0$) and destroys **exergy**.

Key idea: a reversible process is the limit with none of them: frictionless, quasi-equilibrium, with heat transferred across infinitesimal temperature differences.
cards.searchQuery: sources of irreversibility friction heat transfer mixing thermodynamics

cards.title: State the two Carnot principles for heat engines operating between the same two thermal reservoirs.
cards.body:
An irreversible engine is less efficient than a reversible one, and all reversible engines have the same efficiency.

1. An **irreversible** engine is always less efficient than a reversible one between the same two reservoirs.
2. All **reversible** engines between the same two reservoirs have the same efficiency, whatever the working fluid or design.

Key idea: the maximum efficiency depends only on the reservoir temperatures, $\eta_{\text{rev}} = 1 - T_L/T_H$.
cards.searchQuery: Carnot principles heat engines reversible irreversible same efficiency

cards.title: What are the four processes of the Carnot cycle, in order, starting with heat addition?
cards.body:
Isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression, adiabatic compression.

1. Reversible isothermal expansion at $T_H$ (heat in)
2. Reversible adiabatic (isentropic) expansion from $T_H$ to $T_L$
3. Reversible isothermal compression at $T_L$ (heat out)
4. Reversible adiabatic (isentropic) compression from $T_L$ to $T_H$

On a $T$–$s$ diagram it's a rectangle.

Watch out: it's impractical because truly **isothermal** heat transfer is extremely slow.
cards.searchQuery: Carnot cycle four processes isothermal adiabatic order

cards.title: For a completely reversible heat engine, the ratio of heat rejected to heat received, $Q_L/Q_H$, equals what?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{Q_L}{Q_H} = \dfrac{T_L}{T_H}$, with absolute temperatures.

This relation defines the **Kelvin (thermodynamic) temperature scale**, independent of any substance's properties.

It gives $\eta_{\text{rev}} = 1 - T_L/T_H$. For an irreversible engine, $Q_L/Q_H > T_L/T_H$: it rejects more heat.

Tip: this ratio is why efficiency formulas need absolute temperatures.
cards.searchQuery: reversible heat engine QL/QH equals TL/TH Kelvin scale

cards.title: What is the highest possible COP of a refrigerator that keeps a space at $250\,\mathrm{K}$ while rejecting heat to surroundings at $300\,\mathrm{K}$?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{COP_{R,max}} = 5$.

$\mathrm{COP_{R,rev}} = \dfrac{T_L}{T_H - T_L} = \dfrac{250}{50} = 5$.

The bigger the **temperature lift** $T_H - T_L$, the lower the COP: a freezer, lifting heat across a larger difference than a fridge, has a lower COP.

Tip: every real refrigerator has a COP below this Carnot limit.
cards.searchQuery: Carnot refrigerator maximum COP TL/(TH-TL)

cards.title: An engine receives $60\,\mathrm{kJ}$ per cycle from a $1000\,\mathrm{K}$ source and rejects heat to a $300\,\mathrm{K}$ sink. Maximum net work per cycle, in kJ?
cards.body:
$W_{\text{max}} = 42\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

$\eta_{\text{max}} = 1 - \dfrac{300}{1000} = 0.70$, so $W_{\text{max}} = 0.70(60) = 42\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

An inventor claiming $50\,\mathrm{kJ}$ per cycle from this engine would be violating the **second law**, even though the claim satisfies the first.

Tip: to test a claim, compare the claimed $\eta$ with $1 - T_L/T_H$; if it's larger, reject it.
cards.searchQuery: maximum work heat engine Carnot limit inventor claim

cards.title: A refrigerator removes $300\,\mathrm{kJ}$ from its cold space using $100\,\mathrm{kJ}$ of work. How much heat does it reject to the kitchen, in kJ?
cards.body:
$Q_H = 400\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

Energy balance on the cycle: $Q_H = Q_L + W_{\text{in}} = 300 + 100 = 400\,\mathrm{kJ}$, and $\mathrm{**COP**_R} = Q_L/W_{\text{in}} = 3$.

That's why running a refrigerator with its door open heats the kitchen: it rejects more heat than it removes.

Tip: $Q_H = Q_L + W_{\text{in}}$ is just the first law for a cycle.
cards.searchQuery: refrigerator heat rejected QH = QL + W

cards.title: Why can a heat pump with $\mathrm{COP_{HP}} = 3$ heat a house more cheaply than electric resistance heaters?
cards.body:
It delivers $3\,\mathrm{kJ}$ of heat per $1\,\mathrm{kJ}$ of electricity, versus exactly $1\,\mathrm{kJ}$ for a resistance heater.

The extra $2\,\mathrm{kJ}$ isn't created: it's **heat pumped in** from the cold outdoors, and $Q_H = Q_L + W_{\text{in}}$ still holds.

Watch out: the COP drops as the outdoor temperature falls, because the temperature lift grows.
cards.searchQuery: heat pump versus electric resistance heater COP cost

cards.title: An engine has $\eta_{\text{th}} = 30\%$; a reversible engine between the same reservoirs would reach $60\%$. What is its second-law efficiency, in percent?
cards.body:
$\eta_{\text{II}} = 50\%$.

$\eta_{\text{II}} = \dfrac{\eta_{\text{th}}}{\eta_{\text{th,rev}}} = \dfrac{0.30}{0.60} = 0.50$: the engine **achieves half** of what the second law allows.

For refrigerators and heat pumps, $\eta_{\text{II}} = \mathrm{COP}/\mathrm{COP_{rev}}$; for work-consuming devices in general, $\eta_{\text{II}} = W_{\text{rev}}/W_{\text{actual}}$.

Key idea: $\eta_{\text{II}}$ compares the device with the best possible one, not with $100\%$.
cards.searchQuery: second law efficiency actual over reversible

cards.title: Clausius inequality: for any cycle, the cyclic integral $\oint \dfrac{\delta Q}{T}$ is always what?
cards.body:
$\oint \dfrac{\delta Q}{T} \le 0$: equal to zero for **internally reversible** cycles and negative for irreversible ones.

$T$ is the absolute temperature at the part of the boundary where $\delta Q$ crosses.

The equality case is what makes $\left(\dfrac{\delta Q}{T}\right)_{\text{int rev}}$ the differential of a property, entropy.

Key idea: $\oint \delta Q/T = 0$ for reversible cycles, $< 0$ for irreversible ones, and $> 0$ is impossible.
acceptedAnswers: less than or equal to zero
cards.searchQuery: Clausius inequality cyclic integral dQ/T

cards.title: How is the entropy change of a closed system defined in terms of heat transfer?
cards.body:
$\Delta S = \displaystyle\int_1^2 \left(\frac{\delta Q}{T}\right)_{\text{int rev}}$, in $\mathrm{kJ/K}$.

The integral must follow an **internally reversible path**, but $S$ is a property, so any real process between the same two states has the same $\Delta S$.

For an actual process, $\Delta S = \int \dfrac{\delta Q}{T_b} + S_{\text{gen}}$, where $T_b$ is the boundary temperature.

Watch out: $\int \delta Q/T$ along the actual irreversible path is not $\Delta S$; it is smaller.
cards.searchQuery: entropy definition integral dQ/T internally reversible

cards.title: A thermal reservoir at $500\,\mathrm{K}$ supplies $1000\,\mathrm{kJ}$ of heat. What is the reservoir's entropy change, in kJ/K?
cards.body:
$\Delta S = -2\,\mathrm{kJ/K}$.

A reservoir stays at constant $T$, so $\Delta S = Q/T = -1000/500 = -2\,\mathrm{kJ/K}$: **negative** because the heat leaves.

A system's entropy can decrease; the second law only forbids a decrease in the total, including whatever receives the heat.

Example: if the reservoir at $500\,\mathrm{K}$ instead absorbed $1000\,\mathrm{kJ}$, its entropy would rise by $2\,\mathrm{kJ/K}$.
cards.searchQuery: thermal reservoir entropy change Q/T

cards.title: $100\,\mathrm{kJ}$ of heat flows directly from a reservoir at $500\,\mathrm{K}$ to one at $250\,\mathrm{K}$. Total entropy generated, in kJ/K?
cards.body:
$S_{\text{gen}} = 0.2\,\mathrm{kJ/K}$.

$S_{\text{gen}} = \Delta S_{\text{hot}} + \Delta S_{\text{cold}} = -\dfrac{100}{500} + \dfrac{100}{250} = -0.2 + 0.4 = 0.2\,\mathrm{kJ/K}$.

Heat transfer across a **finite temperature difference** is irreversible. Reverse the direction and you'd get $-0.2\,\mathrm{kJ/K}$, which is impossible.

Tip: for heat transfer between two reservoirs, $S_{\text{gen}} = Q\left(\dfrac{1}{T_L} - \dfrac{1}{T_H}\right)$.
cards.searchQuery: entropy generation heat transfer finite temperature difference

cards.title: Write the two Gibbs ($T\,ds$) relations for a simple compressible substance.
cards.body:
$T\,ds = du + P\,dv$ and $T\,ds = dh - v\,dP$.

They relate properties only, so they hold for **any process**, reversible or not, even though they're derived along a reversible path.

They're the starting point for $\Delta s$ of ideal gases and incompressible substances.

Key idea: the Gibbs relations connect $s$ to ordinary properties, so they're the source of all property-based $\Delta s$ formulas.
cards.searchQuery: Gibbs T ds relations du + P dv dh - v dP

cards.title: Entropy change of an ideal gas with constant $c_p$, in terms of $T_1$, $T_2$, $P_1$ and $P_2$?
cards.body:
$s_2 - s_1 = c_p\ln\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} - R\ln\dfrac{P_2}{P_1}$.

The volume form is $s_2 - s_1 = c_v\ln\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} + R\ln\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}$.

Heating raises $s$; at fixed $T$, compressing to a higher pressure lowers it. Use **absolute $T$**, and don't drop the minus sign on the pressure term.

Tip: if the process is isentropic, set the left side to zero to recover $T_2/T_1 = (P_2/P_1)^{R/c_p}$.
cards.searchQuery: ideal gas entropy change cp ln T2/T1 - R ln P2/P1

cards.title: $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ of liquid water ($c = 4.18\,\mathrm{kJ/(kg\cdot K)}$) is heated from $300$ to $360\,\mathrm{K}$. Its entropy change, in kJ/K to three decimals?
cards.body:
$\Delta S \approx 0.762\,\mathrm{kJ/K}$.

**Incompressible substance**: $\Delta S = mc\ln\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = (1)(4.18)\ln 1.2 = 4.18(0.1823) = 0.762\,\mathrm{kJ/K}$.

Watch out: putting Celsius temperatures inside the logarithm gives a badly wrong answer; use kelvins.
cards.searchQuery: entropy change incompressible substance m c ln T2/T1

cards.title: Air ($k = 1.4$) is compressed isentropically from $100\,\mathrm{kPa}$ and $300\,\mathrm{K}$ to $800\,\mathrm{kPa}$. Final temperature, in K to the nearest kelvin?
cards.body:
$T_2 \approx 543\,\mathrm{K}$.

$T_2 = T_1\left(\dfrac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{(k-1)/k} = 300(8)^{0.2857} = 300(1.811) = 543\,\mathrm{K}$.

Watch out: using an **exponent** of $k - 1$ (that's for a volume ratio) or forgetting the exponent altogether.
cards.searchQuery: isentropic compression air final temperature pressure ratio

cards.title: A turbine's isentropic enthalpy drop would be $500\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$, and its isentropic efficiency is $85\%$. Actual work output, in kJ/kg?
cards.body:
$w_a = 425\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$.

$\eta_T = \dfrac{\text{actual work}}{\text{isentropic work}} = \dfrac{h_1 - h_{2a}}{h_1 - h_{2s}}$, so $w_a = 0.85(500) = 425\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$.

Irreversibilities leave the actual exit state at a **higher enthalpy and entropy** than the isentropic one at the same exit pressure.

Watch out: isentropic efficiency compares actual and ideal work at the same inlet state and the same exit pressure.
cards.searchQuery: turbine isentropic efficiency actual work

cards.title: A compressor would need $200\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$ if it were isentropic, and its isentropic efficiency is $80\%$. Actual work input, in kJ/kg?
cards.body:
$w_a = 250\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$.

For compressors and pumps the ratio is **flipped**: $\eta_C = \dfrac{w_s}{w_a} = \dfrac{h_{2s} - h_1}{h_{2a} - h_1}$, so $w_a = 200/0.80 = 250\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$.

Watch out: multiplying instead ($160\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$) would make the real compressor need LESS work than the ideal one.
cards.searchQuery: compressor isentropic efficiency actual work input

cards.title: On a $T$–$s$ diagram, what does the area under an internally reversible process curve represent, and what does the area enclosed by a cycle represent?
cards.body:
Under a process curve: the **heat transfer per unit mass**, $q = \int T\,ds$.

Enclosed by a cycle: the net heat transfer, which equals the net work, $w_{\text{net}}$.

An isentropic process is a vertical line (no heat). These areas apply only to internally reversible processes, just as areas on a $P$–$v$ diagram give work only for quasi-equilibrium ones.

Tip: a rectangle on a $T$–$s$ diagram (Carnot) has area $(T_H - T_L)\,\Delta s$.
cards.searchQuery: T-s diagram area heat transfer net work cycle

cards.title: What does the Mollier diagram plot, and why is it handy for turbines and nozzles?
cards.body:
Enthalpy $h$ against entropy $s$ (an $h$–$s$ diagram).

For an adiabatic steady-flow device, the vertical distance $\Delta h$ is the work (turbine, compressor) or the kinetic-energy change (nozzle), and the horizontal distance $\Delta s$ reflects the irreversibilities.

An **isentropic process is a vertical line**, so the ideal exit state lies straight below the inlet state, on the exit-pressure line.

Tip: read the isentropic exit enthalpy $h_{2s}$ straight down from the inlet point to the exit-pressure line.
cards.searchQuery: Mollier diagram h-s enthalpy entropy turbine

cards.title: Entropy balance for a closed system exchanging heat $Q_k$ at boundary temperatures $T_k$: $\Delta S_{\text{sys}} = \,?$
cards.body:
$\Delta S_{\text{sys}} = \sum \dfrac{Q_k}{T_k} + S_{\text{gen}}$, with $S_{\text{gen}} \ge 0$.

Entropy crosses a boundary only with heat (and with mass, for control volumes); **work carries no entropy**.

For an adiabatic closed system, $\Delta S_{\text{sys}} = S_{\text{gen}} \ge 0$, so its entropy can never decrease.

Key idea: an isolated system is adiabatic with no work or mass exchange, so $\Delta S_{\text{isolated}} = S_{\text{gen}} \ge 0$.
cards.searchQuery: entropy balance closed system entropy generation

cards.title: What is exergy (availability), and what is the dead state?
cards.body:
The maximum useful work obtainable as a system comes to equilibrium with its environment.

That final equilibrium is the **dead state**, typically $T_0 = 25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $P_0 = 1\,\mathrm{atm}$, with no velocity or elevation relative to it; a system there has zero exergy.

Key idea: unlike energy, exergy isn't conserved. Irreversibilities destroy it.
cards.searchQuery: exergy availability dead state maximum useful work

cards.title: A process generates $0.2\,\mathrm{kJ/K}$ of entropy with the environment at $T_0 = 300\,\mathrm{K}$. How much exergy is destroyed, in kJ?
cards.body:
$X_{\text{destroyed}} = 60\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

**Gouy–Stodola theorem**: $X_{\text{destroyed}} = T_0S_{\text{gen}} = 300(0.2) = 60\,\mathrm{kJ}$ of work potential, lost for good.

It's zero for reversible processes and never negative.

Key idea: $X_{\text{destroyed}} = T_0S_{\text{gen}}$ turns entropy generation into lost work potential.
cards.searchQuery: exergy destruction Gouy-Stodola T0 S gen

cards.title: What is the exergy (work potential) of heat $Q$ supplied at a constant temperature $T$, with the environment at $T_0$?
cards.body:
$X_{\text{heat}} = Q\left(1 - \dfrac{T_0}{T}\right)$: the work a **Carnot engine** could extract running between $T$ and $T_0$.

Heat available only slightly above $T_0$ has little work potential, which is why low-temperature waste heat is hard to use.

Example: $100\,\mathrm{kJ}$ at $600\,\mathrm{K}$ with $T_0 = 300\,\mathrm{K}$ has an exergy of $50\,\mathrm{kJ}$.
cards.searchQuery: exergy of heat Carnot engine work potential Q(1 - T0/T)

cards.title: List the four processes of the ideal Otto cycle in order, starting with compression.
cards.body:
Isentropic compression, constant-volume heat addition, isentropic expansion, constant-volume heat rejection.

1. 1→2: isentropic compression
2. 2→3: **constant-volume** heat addition (combustion at top dead center)
3. 3→4: isentropic expansion (the power stroke)
4. 4→1: constant-volume heat rejection (exhaust and intake)

Why: the Otto cycle idealizes a spark-ignition engine by treating combustion as instantaneous, so the piston has no time to move during heat addition.
Tip: on a $T$–$s$ diagram, the two constant-volume processes are curves; the two isentropes are vertical lines.
cards.searchQuery: Otto cycle four processes isentropic constant volume spark ignition

cards.title: In the ideal Diesel cycle, is heat added at constant volume or at constant pressure?
cards.body:
Constant pressure (process 2→3).

The other three processes match the Otto cycle: isentropic compression, isentropic expansion and **constant-volume** heat rejection.

Why: fuel is injected into air that compression has already heated above its ignition temperature (**compression ignition**), and it burns as the piston moves down, roughly holding $P$ constant.
Key idea: with no fuel in the cylinder during compression, there's no knock, so Diesel engines can use compression ratios of about $12$ to $24$.
cards.searchQuery: Diesel cycle heat addition constant pressure compression ignition

cards.title: Cold-air-standard Diesel cycle: thermal efficiency in terms of compression ratio $r$, specific heat ratio $k$ and cutoff ratio $r_c$?
cards.body:
$\eta_{\text{Diesel}} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{r^{k-1}}\left[\dfrac{r_c^{\,k} - 1}{k\,(r_c - 1)}\right]$

The cutoff ratio is $r_c = V_3/V_2$, the volume after heat addition divided by the volume before it. $r_c > 1$ always.

Why: heat is added over a longer part of the stroke than in the Otto cycle, so less of it is added at the top.
Watch out: the bracket is greater than $1$, so at the **same** $r$ the Diesel cycle is less efficient than the Otto cycle. As $r_c \to 1$, it reduces to the Otto formula.
cards.searchQuery: Diesel cycle thermal efficiency formula cutoff ratio compression ratio

cards.title: At the same compression ratio, which ideal cycle has the higher thermal efficiency, Otto or Diesel?
cards.body:
Otto.

At equal $r$, the Diesel cycle has a factor $\dfrac{r_c^{\,k} - 1}{k(r_c - 1)} > 1$ that lowers its efficiency below the Otto value.

In practice Diesel engines are **more** efficient overall, because they run at much higher compression ratios (no knock).
Watch out: a comparison is only fair at equal $r$ or at equal peak pressure; real engines don't operate at equal $r$.
cards.searchQuery: Otto vs Diesel cycle efficiency same compression ratio

cards.title: List the four processes of the ideal Brayton cycle (gas turbine) in order, starting with compression.
cards.body:
Isentropic compression, constant-pressure heat addition, isentropic expansion, constant-pressure heat rejection.

1. 1→2: isentropic compression in the compressor
2. 2→3: constant-pressure heat addition in the combustor
3. 3→4: isentropic expansion in the turbine
4. 4→1: constant-pressure heat rejection to the surroundings

Why: real gas turbines are open cycles, with fresh air in and exhaust out. The ideal cycle closes the loop with a heat-rejection process so the air-standard analysis works.
Tip: the Brayton cycle is the Rankine cycle's gas analog, with a compressor in place of the pump and a combustor in place of the boiler.

cards.title: Ideal Brayton cycle with constant specific heats: thermal efficiency in terms of the pressure ratio $r_p = P_2/P_1$ and $k$?
cards.body:
$\eta_{\text{Brayton}} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{r_p^{(k-1)/k}}$

It rises with the pressure ratio. Equivalently, $\eta = 1 - T_1/T_2$, the temperatures at the compressor inlet and exit.

Why: the isentropic relations give $T_2/T_1 = T_3/T_4 = r_p^{(k-1)/k}$, so the heat ratio $q_{\text{out}}/q_{\text{in}}$ reduces to $T_1/T_2$.
Watch out: the exponent is $(k-1)/k$ for a pressure ratio, not $k-1$.

cards.title: An ideal Brayton cycle with air ($k = 1.4$) has a pressure ratio of $8$. What is its thermal efficiency, in percent to one decimal?
cards.body:
$44.8\%$.

$\eta = 1 - r_p^{-(k-1)/k} = 1 - 8^{-0.2857} = 1 - 0.552 = 0.448$.

Doubling the pressure ratio to $16$ gives $1 - 16^{-0.2857} \approx 0.547$ ($54.7\%$): efficiency keeps rising with $r_p$, but with diminishing returns.
Watch out: the cycle's maximum temperature limits how high $r_p$ can usefully go, since net work eventually falls.

cards.title: What is the back work ratio of a power cycle, and is it large or small for a gas turbine?
cards.body:
The fraction of the turbine's work that's used to drive the compressor or pump: $\mathrm{bwr} = \dfrac{w_{\text{in}}}{w_{\text{out}}}$.

For gas turbines it's **large**, typically about $40$ to $80\%$, because compressing a gas takes a lot of work. In a Rankine cycle it's tiny (a percent or two), because pumping a liquid takes very little.

Why: $w = \int v\,dP$ and the specific volume of a gas is far larger than that of a liquid.
Key idea: net work is the small difference of two large numbers in a gas turbine, so component efficiencies matter a lot.

cards.title: What does a regenerator do in a gas-turbine cycle, and when does it help?
cards.body:
It preheats the compressed air with hot turbine exhaust, so less fuel is needed for the same net work.

It helps only when the turbine exhaust is **hotter** than the compressor exit ($T_4 > T_2$), which means low pressure ratios.

Why: at high pressure ratios $T_2 > T_4$, so heat would flow from the compressed air to the exhaust, the wrong way.
Watch out: a regenerator raises efficiency but doesn't change the net work, since the turbine and compressor work stay the same.

cards.title: In a Rankine cycle with fixed turbine inlet temperature, what does raising the boiler pressure do to the thermal efficiency and to the turbine exit quality?
cards.body:
Efficiency rises, but the turbine exit quality falls (wetter steam).

The average temperature of heat addition goes up, which raises $\eta_{\text{th}}$.

Why: the expansion line ends further into the vapor dome, so more liquid droplets form in the last turbine stages.
Watch out: the exit quality should stay above roughly $0.85$ to $0.90$, because droplets erode turbine blades. Reheat is the usual cure.

cards.title: How does lowering the condenser pressure affect a Rankine cycle's thermal efficiency, and what limits how low it can go?
cards.body:
Efficiency rises, because the average temperature of heat **rejection** falls.

The limit is the temperature of the cooling medium: $T_{\text{sat}}$ in the condenser must stay above the cooling water or air temperature, which sets a minimum saturation pressure.

Why: heat rejection occurs at $T_{\text{sat}}$, and $\eta$ improves as $T_{\text{out}}$ falls.
Watch out: a lower condenser pressure also lowers the turbine exit quality, and it raises the risk of air leaking into the condenser.

cards.title: Why is reheat added to a Rankine cycle, and how does it work?
cards.body:
To cut moisture in the turbine exit steam, which allows a higher boiler pressure.

The steam expands partway through a high-pressure turbine, returns to the boiler to be reheated at **constant pressure**, and then expands in a low-pressure turbine.

Why: the dry exit steam protects the last turbine stages from droplet erosion, and the higher average heat-addition temperature helps efficiency.
Key idea: the gain from reheat is mainly the quality improvement, plus a modest efficiency gain.

cards.title: An ideal Rankine cycle has turbine work $1000\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$, pump work $10\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$ and boiler heat input $3000\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$. What is its thermal efficiency, in percent?
cards.body:
$33\%$.

$w_{\text{net}} = w_{\text{turb}} - w_{\text{pump}} = 1000 - 10 = 990\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$, so $\eta_{\text{th}} = \dfrac{990}{3000} = 0.33$.

Watch out: ignoring the pump gives $33.3\%$; here it's a small effect, but net work always means turbine minus pump.
Tip: $q_{\text{in}} = h_3 - h_2$ is measured from the pump exit, not the condenser exit.

cards.title: List the four components of the ideal vapor-compression refrigeration cycle in flow order, with the ideal process in each.
cards.body:
Compressor, condenser, expansion valve, evaporator.

1. Compressor: isentropic compression of saturated vapor
2. Condenser: constant-pressure heat rejection (ends as saturated liquid)
3. Expansion valve: throttling, so $h_3 = h_4$
4. Evaporator: constant-pressure heat absorption (ends as saturated vapor)

Watch out: the expansion valve is the one irreversible step in the ideal cycle, and it adds no work or heat.
Tip: refrigerant leaves the evaporator and enters the compressor as saturated vapor, never as liquid.

cards.title: In an ideal vapor-compression cycle, $h_1 = 250$ (compressor inlet), $h_2 = 290$ (compressor exit) and $h_3 = h_4 = 90\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$. What is $\mathrm{COP_R}$?
cards.body:
$4$.

$q_L = h_1 - h_4 = 160\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$ and $w_{\text{in}} = h_2 - h_1 = 40\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$, so $\mathrm{COP_R} = \dfrac{h_1 - h_4}{h_2 - h_1} = 4$.

Heat rejected in the condenser: $q_H = h_2 - h_3 = 200\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$. Check: $q_L + w_{\text{in}} = 200$.
Watch out: $h_4$ is the evaporator **inlet**, equal to $h_3$ after the valve, so use $h_4$ (or $h_3$), not $h_2$, in $q_L$.

cards.title: Why do household refrigerators use an expansion valve (or capillary tube) instead of a turbine to expand the refrigerant?
cards.body:
Because a turbine would recover very little work and would cost far more than it saves.

The refrigerant is liquid or a liquid-vapor mixture there, with a small enthalpy drop, and a turbine in two-phase flow is complicated and unreliable.

Why: the valve is cheap and simple, so engineers accept the entropy generation (lost work) for practicality.
Key idea: replacing the valve with an isentropic turbine would raise the COP slightly and increase the cooling effect, but not by enough to justify it.

cards.title: Relative humidity $\phi$ of moist air, in terms of the vapor partial pressure $P_v$ and the saturation pressure $P_g$ at the same temperature?
cards.body:
$\phi = \dfrac{P_v}{P_g}$, with $P_g = P_{\text{sat}}$ at the air's dry-bulb temperature.

It's $1$ ($100\%$) for saturated air, and it falls when the air is **heated** at constant $P_v$.

Example: air at $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($P_g \approx 4.25\,\mathrm{kPa}$) with $P_v = 2.1\,\mathrm{kPa}$ has $\phi \approx 0.49$.
Watch out: relative humidity depends on temperature; the humidity ratio $\omega$ doesn't change when you heat air without adding water.

cards.title: When moist air is cooled at constant pressure, what is the temperature at which condensation first begins called?
cards.body:
The dew point.

It's the saturation temperature of water at the **vapor partial pressure**: $T_{\text{dp}} = T_{\text{sat}}@P_v$.

Why: cooling at constant total pressure keeps $P_v$ fixed until $P_v = P_g$, which is saturation ($\phi = 1$).
Tip: look up the dew point in the steam tables by finding the temperature whose $P_{\text{sat}}$ equals $P_v$.

cards.title: Moist air at a total pressure of $100\,\mathrm{kPa}$ has a vapor partial pressure of $2\,\mathrm{kPa}$. What is the humidity ratio $\omega$, in kg water per kg dry air, to four decimals?
cards.body:
$\omega \approx 0.0127\,\mathrm{kg/kg}$.

$\omega = \dfrac{m_v}{m_a} = 0.622\,\dfrac{P_v}{P - P_v} = 0.622\,\dfrac{2}{100 - 2} = 0.01269$.

The factor $0.622$ is the ratio of molar masses, $M_{\text{water}}/M_{\text{air}} = 18.015/28.97$.
Watch out: the denominator is the dry-air pressure $P - P_v$, not the total pressure $P$.

cards.title: Methane burns completely with theoretical air. How many kmol of air are needed per kmol of $\ce{CH4}$? (Air $= \ce{O2 + 3.76N2}$; give two decimals.)
cards.body:
$9.52\,\mathrm{kmol}$ of air per kmol of fuel.

$\ce{CH4 + 2(O2 + 3.76N2) -> CO2 + 2H2O + 7.52N2}$

Two kmol of $\ce{O2}$ are needed, and each comes with $3.76$ kmol of $\ce{N2}$: $2(1 + 3.76) = 9.52$.

Key idea: **theoretical (stoichiometric) air** is the minimum air for complete combustion; the products contain no free $\ce{O2}$.
Watch out: the nitrogen is inert in the balance but isn't negligible: it carries heat out with the exhaust.
cards.searchQuery: methane combustion theoretical air kmol per kmol stoichiometric

cards.title: What is the mass air–fuel ratio for methane burned with theoretical air? ($M_{\text{air}} = 28.97$, $M_{\ce{CH4}} = 16.04\,\mathrm{kg/kmol}$; one decimal.)
cards.body:
$\mathrm{AF} \approx 17.2\,\mathrm{kg}$ air per kg fuel.

$\mathrm{AF} = \dfrac{m_{\text{air}}}{m_{\text{fuel}}} = \dfrac{(9.52)(28.97)}{(1)(16.04)} = \dfrac{275.8}{16.04} \approx 17.2$.

Use the kmol counts from the balanced reaction, then convert each to mass with the molar masses.
Watch out: the mole ratio ($9.52$) and the mass ratio ($17.2$) differ, because air and methane have different molar masses.
